=== 2. Stress and Resistance ===

1. The Concept of Stress The concept of stress is no less complex than the concepts of health and illness, and it has an equally significant history of study in medical and behavioral sciences.

The famous Persian scientist, philosopher, and physician Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980-1037 AD) once conducted an experiment,

the essence of which was that two lambs from the same litter were placed in two different cages, fed and cared for in exactly the same way. But one of the lambs could see a cage containing a wolf. At the beginning of the experiment, both lambs had approximately the same weight and appearance. After some time, the lamb that did not see the wolf was lively and well-fed. The other, who constantly saw the wolf, was thin, depressed, sluggish, and its wool looked unhealthy. After some time, it died. With this experiment, Avicenna showed the connection between chronic negative emotional experiences and health status, extending his conclusions to humans. Here we will touch upon only a few of the most significant models of stress to demonstrate the general course of development of this concept, which continues to this day

As discussed in previous lessons, non-communicable diseases can result from many factors: on the one hand, negative circumstances in which a person finds themselves, and on the other hand, the capabilities of a person's internal resources to resist these negative circumstances. All these internal and external factors, simultaneously affecting health status, have received a special name in behavioral sciences – stress, which has come to be considered the main predictor not only of chronic diseases but also of all types of behavior that violate certain social norms. Accordingly, reducing stress levels has become the main goal of preventing chronic diseases and all types of deviant behavior.

For a preliminary classification of approaches to understanding stress, the following is most common:

Stress as a stimulus or an event in the environment requiring increased expenditure of resources and reactions. Stress as a reaction – general adaptation syndrome. Stress as an interaction between the organism (personality) and the environment. 2. Psychophysiological Model of Stress Walter Cannon (1871 — 1945)

— an American physiologist, professor, and head of the Department of Physiology at Harvard Medical School, widely known for coining the term "fight or flight" in 1915 to describe an animal's reaction to threats in his work "Bodily Changes in Pain, Hunger, Fear and Rage: An Account of Recent Researches into the Function of Emotional Excitement." In this work, Cannon argued that not only physical emergencies, such as blood loss due to injury, but also psychological emergencies, such as conflicts between members of the same species, cause the release of adrenaline, noradrenaline, and cortisol into the bloodstream.

In 1932, in his book "The Wisdom of the Body," he proposed the term homeostasis as the name for "coordinated physiological processes which maintain most of the steady states in the organism." For example, adrenaline, by acting on various organs, performs various adaptive functions, maintaining homeostasis in the body in a dangerous situation. In the skeletal muscles of the limbs, adrenaline relaxes blood vessels, which increases local blood flow. Adrenaline constricts blood vessels in the skin and minimizes blood loss from physical injury. Adrenaline also releases a key metabolic fuel, glucose, from the liver into the bloodstream, and so on.

Hans Selye (1907 — 1982)

– a Canadian pathologist and endocrinologist of Austro-Hungarian origin. He developed the hypothesis of the general adaptation syndrome, according to which a pathogenic factor, such as an infection, has a triggering effect, activating adaptation mechanisms developed during evolution (fever, weakness, loss of appetite). In 1936, he published a short article in the prestigious journal Nature titled "A Syndrome Produced by Diverse Nocuous Agents."

Selye, following Walter Cannon, extended his initial findings in biochemistry to the principles of psychophysiological stress development, viewing it as a response to any demands placed on the organism: no matter what difficulty the organism faced, it could be dealt with by two types of reactions – a) active, or fight, and b) passive, in the form of fleeing from difficulties or readiness to endure them. Experiments on rats showed that they exhibited the same reaction to poisoning as to heat or cold. Other researchers found a similar reaction in people who had suffered extensive burns.

Selye did not imbue stress with psychological meaning: it does not matter whether the stressor is pleasant (pleasure) or not (despair); its effect depends on the "intensity of the demand" placed on the organism's "adaptive capacity," initially implying only humoral reactions of the body.

Selye described the stages characterizing the stress syndrome or general adaptation syndrome. It develops in three consecutive stages, for which characteristic changes in neuroendocrine functioning are described:

initially, the "alarm reaction," during which defensive forces are mobilized; this is the stage of acute manifestations; then comes the "stage of resistance," which reflects full adaptation to the stressor; and finally, the "stage of exhaustion"; characterized by the suppression of organic functions.

In 1956, Selye's work, which soon made him famous, "The Stress of Life," was published, where he wrote: "The idea of the concept of stress and the general adaptation syndrome came to me in 1925 when I was studying medicine at the University of Prague. [...] I crammed myself with the maximum amount of theoretical knowledge and was burning with enthusiasm for the art of healing [...]. What struck me, as a novice, was that apparently very few symptoms characterized each disease; [...] I could not understand why, from the very beginning of medical history, doctors focused all their efforts on recognizing individual diseases and discovering specific remedies, paying no attention to something more obvious: 'the syndrome of simply being sick.' Is it possible to analyze this 'general syndrome of illness' and perhaps even find remedies capable of acting on the non-specific factor(s) of illness?"

Initially, Selye viewed stress exclusively as a destructive, negative phenomenon, but later introduced the additional concept of "positive stress" (eustress), and designated "negative stress" as distress. Unlike short-term stress, whose evolutionary adaptive meaning lies in mobilizing the organism in a dangerous situation, Selye distinguished prolonged stress, which has a suppressive effect on the body.

Throughout his career, Selye identified various components involved in the onset and development of stress, leading him to formulate the concept of "adaptive energy" — a certain volume of the organism's adaptive capabilities that also determines life expectancy. In developing his ideas, he focused his reflections on the "evolution of intercellular altruism" during embryogenesis with "communities of interest."

3. Medical Model of Stress Harold Wolff

(1898-1962) - an American physician, neurologist, considered a pioneer in modern headache research and the study of psychosomatic diseases. He proposed the "stress and illness" model (1953), which relies on the connection between social changes and changes in patterns of psychosomatic diseases. In contemporary (for the author) American culture, sources of stress include industrialization and its accompanying social displacements, conflict due to competition for social benefits, changes in family structure, and intra-family relationships.

Illness is viewed as a reaction to threats from the social environment. This environment is interpreted in cultural dimensions. Culturally generated pressure initiates anxiety, reflecting an individual's perception of culturally acceptable ways to resolve anxiety. These ways are disrupted when the traditional social structure is destroyed.

An individual's reaction to cultural pressure is symbolic and is determined, along with their constitutional-genetic characteristics, by past social experience of experiencing threat and conflict, including that acquired through learning in the parental family.

Social stress has a damaging effect only due to its symbolic nature. That is, social factors themselves do not have a stress-inducing effect if they do not have corresponding meaning for the individual. Chronic stress precedes illness. One disease can have many social and psychological causes, and one social or psychological cause can lead to different diseases. The reaction to stress is not very specific and is relatively predictable only for extremely pronounced personality types. In Wolff's understanding, psychosomatic illness encompasses an extremely wide range of pathological manifestations, including infectious diseases. Analyzing historical trends in changing disease patterns, Wolff first drew attention to the increase in the incidence of tuberculosis and meningococcal meningitis during periods of social crises, linking this increase to a decrease in the body's resistance to infectious agents. In a study of combat stress during World War II, the author showed the significance of threat anticipation; in a study of Korean War veterans, the significance of the demoralization factor; and in an analysis of data on the medical consequences of the Siege of Leningrad, the impact of the breakdown of significant interpersonal relationships. The "stress and illness" model formed the basis of the vast majority of modern empirical socio-psychological studies of stress.

The model of the influence of socio-psychological factors on health by D. Gentry and S. Kobasa (1984) summarizes modern understandings of the mechanisms of this impact. Health risk is subject to the interplay of psychosocial sensitivity and resistance factors, which interact at both social and psychological levels of an individual's life experience. In case of imbalance, a high load on sensitivity occurs with a decrease in resistance. Resistance is represented by three types of variables – hardiness, coping experience, and social support, which act as mediators for the probability of developing illness under stress.

At the individual level, the model includes biological sensitivity and resistance, for example, constitutional predisposition and physical exercise. Most mediators of the stress-illness relationship also exist at the individual level. These are perceptions, attitudes, and coping styles. The action of social factors is indirect and primarily involves strengthening or facilitating the use of psychological resources.

K. Menninger's (1954) Concept of Stress Resistance as Tiers of Defense

HEALTH (adaptation)

1. Awareness of stress. A breach of the first line of defense leads to behaviors such as hypervigilance, hyperexcitability, obsessions, etc. 2. Withdrawal and dissociation, displacement (prejudices), substitution (including magic, fortune-telling, seeking healers) 3. Formation of neurotic symptoms (insomnia, headache, discomfort in internal organs, increased irritability, reactivity) 4. Addictive behavior (dependent): alcohol, drug, overeating 5. Psychopathies – personality disorder that hinders normal human functioning or pathological accentuation of personality traits 6. Functional psychoses, i.e., reversible psychotic states arising under the influence of various causes, including endogenous ones, but in the absence of organic disorders 7. Organic nature of mental disorders 8. Death

ILLNESS (disintegration)

Erich Lindemann's "Grief Work"

Acute grief syndrome – a set of characteristic signs of psychological and somatic symptoms arising immediately or delayed after any crisis or emergency. Development (each stage lasts from 1-2 weeks to 2-3 months):

Disbelief in what happened. Realization of the actual loss – acute phase (tears, etc.). Stage of searching. The person comes to the site of the disaster or the grave. There is no full sense of loss. Reconciliation. Latent phase, when new behavioral mechanisms mature. Compensatory phase or phase of deviant behavior. The person tries to be outside the home more. Compensates with known behaviors (drinking, infidelity, etc., but understands there is no solace). Integration phase – adequate compensation (loss of husband – new marriage). "Grief work" involves helping a person go through these phases (about 1 year). If the grief work is not done adequately, the person gets stuck in a certain phase. Anticipatory grief. For example, wives whose husbands are fighting in wars or working in dangerous professions always live in a situation of anticipating loss. This is morally very difficult. They do grief work while their husband is alive. Family rehabilitation is important.

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's "Grief Work"

Stages of a patient's awareness of a terminal diagnosis – the need to organize interaction with the patient according to these stages

Denial. The patient cannot believe that this has truly happened to them. They go to doctors to recheck the diagnosis or do not believe doctors at all. Anger (protest). Indignation at the doctors' work, hatred towards healthy people. "Why did this happen to me?" "How could this have happened?" Bargaining. An attempt to make a deal with fate. A sharp narrowing of a person's life horizon. Patients might wish, for example, that they will recover if a coin lands on heads. Turning to God, mysticism. Depression. The person understands the full gravity of their situation. They give up, stop fighting, avoid their usual friends, abandon their routine activities, shut themselves in at home, and mourn their fate. During this period, relatives often feel guilt. Acceptance. Patients mobilize their efforts to continue living meaningfully for their loved ones, despite the illness. "I have lived an interesting and full life. Now I can die."

4. Engineering Model of Stress The history of health psychology's development is largely linked to the development of organizational psychology, which addressed the tasks of increasing labor productivity in large enterprises.

Problems in enterprises addressed by psychologists: absenteeism (truancy, tardiness), defects, industrial injuries, theft and property damage, common colds, industrial alcoholism, industrial neuroses, alcohol abuse and psychosomatic diseases, conflicts and strikes, career counseling for managers, participation in recruitment for senior management positions, staff motivation.

One of the first major projects in this field is considered to be the famous Hawthorne Experiment, conducted in the USA in the 1930s. This was a series of large-scale studies involving many thousands of workers and management personnel of large enterprises, during which it was proven that, in addition to physical environmental conditions, psychological factors, particularly the socio-psychological climate in the team, influence labor productivity. Reliable data were obtained on the connection, for example, between social stress and industrial injuries or the level of "cold" (acute respiratory) diseases. The Hawthorne Experiment initiated the study of stress in organizational behavior, which subsequently largely became the basis for the development of preventive health programs.

In the late 1950s, based on the results of a series of health surveys of employees in the aerospace industry in the USA, an engineering model of stress was developed. The model is based on the role concept of personality, which asserts that people behave in accordance with role expectations determined by statuses within an organization. In this process of role interaction, three main situations can arise that lead to a high level of organizational stress:

Role conflict (a person performs several roles simultaneously, and they contradict each other or are incompatible. Lower-level managers often experience role conflict, as they are forced to simultaneously obey the orders of superiors and the demands of ordinary specialists in the organization, for example, production foremen); Role ambiguity (clearly structured role expectations are absent. Specialists in positions with "blurred" functionality find themselves in such a position, for example, creative directors, development directors, etc.); Role overload (when more demands are placed on an employee than can actually be physically fulfilled. Leaders of organizations and departments are more often subject to role overload than others, especially during periods of instability).

It can be said that the three situations listed reflect central organizational variables on which all other socio-psychological indicators in a team depend – organizational climate, emotional burnout, interaction between management and subordinates, relationships between colleagues, conflict resolution strategies, employee job satisfaction, and many others. To a large extent, it is precisely based on these three parameters of organizational behavior that methods for diagnosing and preventing stress in organizations have been developed and are still in use today.

Model of Resistance to Industrial Stress by J. Hackman and E. Lawler (1971)

1. Personal responsibility for work results. Accompanied by a sense of individual success and increased self-esteem. 2. Autonomy. When high, employees experience the results of their efforts as success or failure; when low, they attribute success and failure either to job characteristics or to other employees. 3. Internal subjective significance of work results. The more successful the efforts and the more one manages to apply one's skills and abilities, the more positive an employee's self-perception becomes. 4. Feedback from the production task (task identity, the employee's ability to evaluate the results of their work). 5. Feedback from others (personal identity, i.e., the employee's ability to form an adequate self-assessment based on others' evaluations of work results). 6. The extent to which performing this work requires contact with others. 7. Opportunities for establishing informal friendly relationships with others.

The presence of these elements protects against stress. A lack of them impairs mental health.

Model of Professional Burnout, C. Maslach and S. Jackson (1978)

Professional burnout is a special psychological state, the main feature of which is the devaluation of the core professional values of one's work in the eyes of the individual. Burnout is associated with experiencing professional overload as a stress factor. The term "burnout" ("emotional burnout") itself was proposed by American psychiatrist H. Freudenberger in 1974.

The emotional burnout test was created by American researchers C. Maslach and S. Jackson in 1978, based on their multifactorial theory of burnout, which includes an assessment of the nature of workload, the level of support from management and colleagues, work-rest schedules, the correspondence of job content to internal goals, etc.

Based on the research results, a person receives scores on three scales:

Stage 1. "Emotional Exhaustion": reduced emotional tone, fatigue, sharp mood swings, loss of positive impressions.

Stage 2. "Depersonalization": emotional detachment from others, self-isolation, indifference, formal performance of professional duties without personal involvement or empathy.

Stage 3. "Reduced Personal Accomplishment": dissatisfaction with oneself as a person and as a professional. Negative assessment of one's competence and productivity and, as a consequence, decreased professional motivation, increased negativism towards official duties, a tendency to shirk responsibility, to isolate oneself from others, detachment and non-participation, avoiding work first psychologically, then physically.

Recommendations for the prevention and overcoming of emotional burnout are built on these same grounds.

5. Psychological Model of Stress The creation of the most general psychological model of stress, taking into account the role of both emotional and cognitive mechanisms in its formation, is largely associated with the names of American psychologists Richard Lazarus (1922 – 2002) and his predecessor – Magda Arnold (1903 – 2002).

Lazarus proceeded from the understanding of the connection between stress and emotions, developed by M. Arnold (1967). In their research, they assumed that stress is an emotional reaction that, however, does not exist outside of cognitive processes, without an intellectual assessment of threat. Stress arises if we perceive something in the surrounding reality as a threat. The perception of threat is determined by two stages of appraisal:

a) primary (emotional) appraisal – direct assessment of the objective characteristics of a threatening event (e.g., a car speeding towards us or a breakup with a partner, etc.);

b) secondary (cognitive) appraisal – a person's assessment of their ability to avoid the threat (e.g., the possibility of avoiding a car collision or the likelihood of finding a better partner).

It is important to note that if the secondary appraisal shows that the chances of overcoming the threat are high, then despite any level of primary appraisal, a stress reaction will not occur! Lazarus himself called this model of stress transactional, meaning that stress always arises at the interface of a person's inner world with their social environment, which determines the cognitive and emotional context of experiencing a stressful event.

R. Lazarus's Concept of Stress Coping (Concept of Coping Strategies) (R. Lazarus "Psychological Stress and Coping Process", 1966)

A) Problem-focused (working with the problem, aimed at its solution) — this includes information gathering, time management, planning, adherence to doctor's prescriptions, plans, etc. (a total of 11 coping actions); B) Emotion-focused (working with the attitude towards the problem at the level of relieving negative emotions). This includes humor, relaxation, religion, support for alcoholization, social comparison, focusing on positive aspects, etc. (a total of 62 coping actions). Among psychological models, stress resistance, as a set of personality traits, can be highlighted as follows.

Marie Jahoda's (1958) concept of positive mental health, which identified criteria for psychological health: attitude towards the "Self," growth, development and self-actualization, personal integration, autonomy, perception of reality, mastery and competence in relation to the environment.

Indicators of mental health, S. Kasl (1974): reflecting a sociological orientation – performance of social roles (absence of hospitalization, leaving work or spouse, etc.); reflecting psychological well-being – positive self-image and stable self-concept; reflecting a humanistic orientation – self-actualization in real activity; Absence of pathology.

The research cycle on "hardiness" — a personal style of stress resistance by S. Kobasa, Maddi, and others (1979) demonstrated the structure of attitudes and skills that contribute to transforming a stress situation into an opportunity to manifest one's capabilities. Hardiness, as the ability to resist stress, is considered in three aspects: from the perspective of the emotional-volitional sphere, from the perspective of the cognitive sphere, and as openness to new experience, respectively:

commitment is defined as "the conviction that involvement in what is happening provides the maximum chance to find something worthwhile and interesting for the individual." A person with a developed commitment component enjoys their own activities, during which they feel their significance and value; control represents the conviction that struggle allows one to influence the outcome of events, even if this influence is not absolute and success is not guaranteed, while the opposite of this is a feeling of helplessness, an inability to plan one's actions to control the situation; challenge is a person's conviction that everything that happens to them contributes to their development through knowledge gained from experience – regardless of whether it is positive or negative. A person who views life as a way of gaining experience is willing to act in the absence of reliable guarantees of success, at their own risk, considering the pursuit of simple comfort and security to impoverish one's life. At the core of challenge is the idea of development through active assimilation of knowledge from experience and its subsequent use. This component allows the individual to remain open to the surrounding world and to accept unfolding events as a challenge and a test.

6 The "Stress-Diathesis" Model

The biopsychosocial model includes a general theoretical model of disease etiology, known as the "stress-diathesis" model. All factors of the external social environment are operationalized in this model under the rubric of stress. The impact of stress itself very rarely acts as the actual causal (etiological) factor of a specific disease or group of diseases. For the pathogenic effect of stress to manifest, a corresponding state of the individual is necessary — the so-called "diathesis." Factors that increase an individual's susceptibility to illness are divided into: predisposition factors and precipitation factors.

The model posits the following theses, which are a development of Engel's biopsychosocial model.

Illness cannot be explained by biological factors alone. Stress is a psychosocial factor mediated by the perception and appraisal of a stressful event. The interaction of psychosocial factors with diathesis (predisposition) explains and localizes the causes of disease.

7. Sources and Factors of Socio-Psychological Stress In health psychology, the following types of stress sources are conceptualized:

Gender-role factors (male and female social roles). Age and life cycle (age crises) Family structure (family risk factors, health as the ability to create and maintain a family) Childhood and adolescence factors (adolescent deviance) Organizational (industrial) factors (physical and psychological working conditions, career) Socio-economic status (belonging to a certain stratum corresponds to health status). Cultural norms (determine standards of health and illness-related behavior, ethnic, religious norms). Territorial factors (identity with a community, specific territorial factors) Social changes (economic booms and busts, political changes affect morbidity rates) Geographical and socio-stratificational mobility (economic horizontal and vertical mobility, external migration and refugees). The above-listed sources of socio-psychological stress can lead to various types of individual, group, or organizational deviant behavior. And each of these stress sources can be described through many factors, the study of which is the domain of health psychology. A more detailed history of their study can be found in Gurvich, 1999, pp. 132-403.

The closest word in meaning to "factor" is "cause," which determines the state of some object of study. In health psychology (following medicine), factors are understood as causes that determine the health-illness state of an individual or a social group. And the main question here is — why do we need to know about the factors of illness, deviant behavior, or some social problem? The answer is that the purpose of prevention is to change someone's behavior towards a healthier one. But influencing behavior actually means influencing the factors that determine (govern) that behavior. Therefore, these factors must be known so that prevention efforts can be directed precisely at them.

Furthermore, factors serve to predict the emergence and development of a problem. For example, by knowing the factors of drug use, one can predict the likelihood of a specific person starting to use drugs based on their presence or absence, even before the first drug trial occurs. This provides an opportunity to offer timely professional help.

Human behavior is complex, so there is no single critically significant risk factor that could predict the onset of high stress levels in a particular person; it is always formed under the influence of a complex combination of many factors. A cumulative effect exists: the more risk factors present in an adolescent's life, and the longer they are exposed to their influence, the greater the likelihood of developing deviant behavior. Furthermore, different risk factors tend to reinforce each other. However, factors remain merely probabilities! Some people maintain "hardiness" and healthy behavior even in very unfavorable conditions.

Risk factors can have both direct and indirect effects on the overall level of juvenile delinquency. For example, poverty. In addition to lowering the quality of life itself, it can also act as an indirect risk factor because it creates emotional tension for parents, which can affect family relationships, reduce the amount of attention directed towards the child, ultimately leading to family breakdown and increasing the risk of a child developing criminal behavior.

It should be noted that in each territory and in each educational organization, the significance of the listed sources of stress and their contribution to the formation of deviant behavior will differ. Therefore, when planning preventive programs, special studies of youth groups with whom work is planned are required to identify factors that are relevant to them at the present time. For this purpose, research procedures will be discussed in the second module of the course.
